title: From Phoolan to Nagaland's First Feature, Indian Cinema Takes Over Toronto
excerpt: Months after Cannes selected no Indian film in any section, the Toronto International Film Festival has programmed Indian titles across five sections — from Richie Mehta's Phoolan to a 4K restoration of John Abraham's 1986 Malayalam classic Amma Ariyan.
body:
• TIFF's 2026 lineup, the 51st edition running September 10–20, features Indian films across five sections — months after no Indian film was selected at Cannes in May.
  • Richie Mehta's Phoolan, on the life of outlaw Phoolan Devi, premieres in Special Presentations; Theja Rio's Angh, the first feature film from Nagaland, is in Platform Competition.
  • Karthik Subbaraj's Dorothy, produced by Guneet Monga, gets a Centrepiece world premiere, and Rahul Roye's short Aman is in the Short Cuts program.
  • A 4K restoration of John Abraham's 1986 Malayalam classic Amma Ariyan (Report to Mother) headlines the TIFF Classics program.

The Toronto International Film Festival has given Indian cinema what Cannes would not: a lineup. Months after no Indian film was selected for any section at Cannes in May, TIFF's 2026 program arrived with Indian titles spread across five sections, touching on subjects as varied as caste violence in rural Tamil Nadu, a vanishing way of life in Nagaland, and India's most famous outlaw.

The headline titles

In the Special Presentations section, director Richie Mehta is premiering Phoolan, the story of a 17-year-old girl who dared to resist patriarchy — becoming the most famous outlaw in Indian history and the target of 2,000 heavily armed men sent to kill her. The film captures a brutal 48-hour siege that, by design, defies the conventions of action cinema. Mehta has said he believes a festival audience arrives with a broad awareness of the world and will engage with the film not as a period piece, but as something that speaks to the present.

Angh, the debut feature from Nagaland-born filmmaker Theja Rio, is selected in the Platform Competition. Set among the Konyak community in the early 1960s, it follows a village chief who stays behind, tending to an ailing wife and a son who does not speak, as the world around him changes irrevocably. Shot entirely on 16-millimeter by Polish cinematographer Adam Pietkiewicz — who is being honoured with the festival's Variety Artisan Award — the film is in Konyak, a language spoken only by the Konyak tribe, and is the first feature film from Nagaland.

A restored classic returns

The Classics program carries the year's most significant rediscovery: John Abraham's Report to Mother (Amma Ariyan, 1986), the Malayalam cult classic, in a meticulous new 4K restoration receiving its North American premiere. Abraham (1937–1987), a legendary figure of Indian parallel cinema and protege of Ritwik Ghatak, made the film as his final work.

Set in 1970s Kerala, it follows Purushan, who encounters the body of a young man who has taken his own life and journeys — with a group of companions that progressively swells — to inform the dead man's mother. The film traverses the geography and social strata of Kerala, mapping the state's political unrest as a form of collective ritual, and is widely regarded as one of the most significant works of political cinema from the subcontinent.

New work in the main sections

The Centrepiece program — TIFF's main section, with 54 titles from 50 countries this year — includes the world premiere of Dorothy, directed by Karthik Subbaraj and produced by Guneet Monga. In the Short Cuts program, Rahul Roye's Aman, an India-UK-USA-France production, will have its world premiere. The 51st edition of the festival, presented by Rogers, runs September 10–20.

Why Toronto matters

Toronto is one of the few major festivals where Indian cinema has a built-in audience. The city is home to huge immigrant communities from India, and Indian films have long sold out screenings at the festival — the city that first premiered Slumdog Millionaire has a documented appetite for stories rooted in the subcontinent.

The contrast with Cannes is hard to miss. After a May shutout on the French Riviera, the breadth of the Toronto selection — from a restored parallel-cinema landmark to a first feature in a tribal language — suggests that the international festival circuit's centre of gravity for Indian cinema, at least this year, sits in Canada.
nri_angle: Toronto is home to one of the largest Indian diaspora communities in the world, where Indian films routinely sell out at TIFF — for many NRIs, the festival's Indian lineup is a first look at the films that will dominate conversation back home and on streaming.
author: Diaspora Desk
